findings.title: canManage() on all groups is granted by the VIEW scope
findings.body: canManage() checks hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE), so an admin who holds only the 'view' scope on all groups is treated as able to manage groups. addTopLevelGroup calls requireManage(), so a view-only admin can create top-level groups. Only MANAGE should be checked here. The Javadoc on GroupPermissionEvaluator.canManage() repeats the mistake by saying 'VIEW or MANAGE'.

findings.title: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission passes resource id where the group id is expected
findings.body: hasPermission(groupId, ...) looks up the resource with resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId), because V2 group resources are named by group id. The lambda passes groupResource.getId(), which is the resource UUID and differs from the name. The lookup misses, falls back to the all-groups resource, and yields wrong results. The granted set also holds resource ids instead of group ids, and callers pass it to user searches as group ids. It should use groupResource.getName().

findings.title: Possible NPE when the all-groups resource type resource is missing
findings.body: getResourceTypeResource can return null, for example when the schema is unsupported or the resource is not found. The code then calls policyStore.findByResource(server, resource) and resource.getScopes() on the null value without a check. The same pattern exists in UserPermissionsV2.

findings.title: V1 group view filtering behavior changed
findings.body: UsersResource and BruteForceUsersResource now always set UserModel.GROUPS from getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, even for callers who can view all users. In V1 that case returns an empty set and the attribute is skipped, so it is probably fine. However, the old `!auth.users().canView()` guard was dropped. Previously canManage() also short-circuited this path; it is now covered only by canView(), which does include the manage-users role. The behavior is subtle and untested.
